summary: The WebSocket protocol enables two-way real-time communication between clients and servers where direct TCP and UDP are not available, such as in a browser. This proposed standard defines a WebSocket subprotocol as a reliable transport for the Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP), so messaging can happen from web clients.

plainLanguage.summary: Web pages cannot always use the usual plumbing for chat sessions. This lets chat messages ride inside a two-way web connection that a browser can open.

questions: how does msrp work in a browser
what is the websocket msrp subprotocol
why must msrp websocket use a relay
subtitle: How chat-style MSRP messages ride inside a WebSocket connection so web clients can use them.

tldr.problem: Code running in a web browser cannot open direct TCP or UDP connections, so it cannot speak the Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP) the usual way.
tldr.mechanism: A new WebSocket subprotocol named msrp carries MSRP requests and responses, one MSRP chunk per WebSocket message, over a secure WebSocket connection to an MSRP relay.
tldr.outcome: Web clients and other WebSocket-capable apps can take part in MSRP sessions, always through a relay that acts as the WebSocket server. The document also updates RFC 4975 and RFC 4976.

today: RFC 7977 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 4975 and RFC 4976, and it registered the msrp subprotocol with IANA.

sections.title: Why MSRP Needs WebSocket
sections.content:
The WebSocket protocol (RFC 6455) lets clients and servers exchange messages in both directions over one persistent TCP connection, optionally secured with TLS. Its opening handshake uses HTTP, so it can reuse existing web infrastructure. Web browsers include a WebSocket client, and the RFC expects other client applications, such as those on smartphones, to offer one too.

RFC 7977 uses that connection to carry the Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP, RFC 4975). It defines three things: a new WebSocket subprotocol, a new transport for MSRP, and procedures for MSRP clients and relays that use it.

The RFC lists typical uses: human-to-machine messaging, client-to-server data exchange such as application control signaling, and human-to-human messaging where local policy requires authentication or logging. MSRP Connection Establishment for Media Anchoring (MSRP-CEMA) is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Web pages are not allowed to use the usual chat pipes. This document shows how to send chat messages through a pipe that web pages can use.

sections.title: WebSocket in Brief
sections.content:
A WebSocket connection starts as an HTTP GET request with an Upgrade header. If the server accepts, it answers with HTTP status 101, and the same TCP connection then carries WebSocket messages in both directions. Unlike plain HTTP, the connection is persistent and can be used for many exchanges.

During the handshake the two sides agree on an application protocol, called a WebSocket subprotocol, that defines the format and meaning of the messages. WebSocket preserves message boundaries. A message can hold UTF-8 text or binary data, and the WebSocket stack may split it into several frames.

The browser WebSocket API only reports a message once the whole message has arrived, whether it came in one frame or several.
sections.plainLanguage: A WebSocket is like a phone call that stays connected, instead of sending a letter each time. Both people can talk whenever they like.

sections.title: Negotiating the msrp Subprotocol
sections.content:
The client MUST include the value msrp in the Sec-WebSocket-Protocol header of its handshake request. The server's 101 reply MUST contain msrp in its own Sec-WebSocket-Protocol header. After that, every WebSocket message on the connection MUST conform to the msrp subprotocol.

An MSRP WebSocket Client is an MSRP entity that opens outbound connections to MSRP relays that are WebSocket servers. An MSRP WebSocket Server is specifically an MSRP relay (RFC 4976) that listens for such connections.
sections.plainLanguage: When the call connects, the browser says it wants to speak 'msrp', and the server says 'fine, me too'. After that they must stick to that language.

sections.title: Carrying MSRP Messages
sections.content:
WebSocket clients cannot receive connections started by other WebSocket clients or servers, so a direct client-to-client MSRP path is hard. Therefore all MSRP-over-WebSocket messages MUST be routed through an MSRP WebSocket Server. That server can route between WebSocket clients and between a WebSocket client and ordinary MSRP clients and relays.

Each MSRP chunk MUST be carried in a single WebSocket message, and a WebSocket message MUST NOT contain more than one chunk. This keeps parsing simple. When a non-WebSocket peer sends a large message, the server MUST use MSRP chunking to split it into smaller chunks.

MSRP allows text and binary bodies, so clients and servers MUST accept both text and binary WebSocket frames. The browser API will not send non-UTF-8 characters in a text frame, and the content of text frames MUST be interpreted as binary.
sections.plainLanguage: Each little piece of a chat message goes in its own envelope, and every envelope holds exactly one piece. Anything big gets cut into smaller pieces first.

sections.title: URIs and SDP Changes
sections.content:
The RFC adds the value ws as a transport parameter for an MSRP URI that is reached through the WebSocket subprotocol. The updated ABNF is transport = "tcp" / "ws" / 1*ALPHANUM.

No new SDP transport protocol is defined. Because all traffic goes through a WebSocket server, the client MUST put TCP/TLS/MSRP in the SDP m-line, the same as non-WebSocket clients and relays. The ws parameter appears in the URI in the SDP path attribute. MSRP was designed to allow new transports, so implementations are expected to tolerate unrecognized ones, provided they do not have to connect directly to that resource.
sections.plainLanguage: The address of a web client gets a small tag, 'ws', so everyone knows to reach it through the web connection. The session description still uses the old wording so older software is not confused.

sections.title: Authenticating the Connection
sections.content:
RFC 4976 said AUTH requests MUST be authenticated. RFC 7977 widens this: all connections between MSRP clients and relays MUST be authenticated. A WebSocket client has three options: HTTP Digest in the AUTH request, a cookie or HTTP Digest during the WebSocket handshake, or mutual TLS between client and server.

During the handshake the server MAY inspect HTTP headers such as Cookie, Host or Origin, or reply with a 401. If the request has an Origin header, the server SHOULD add an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header to the 101 response. Even if the handshake needs no authentication, the server MAY challenge an AUTH request with a 401, so clients SHOULD support HTTP Digest.

An AUTH request is still required when authentication happens at the WebSocket level, because the Use-Path header needed for the SDP offer comes in the 200 OK reply to AUTH. A browser cannot learn its local address, so the client builds a random name ending in .invalid for the host part of its From-Path URI. That is safe because a relay does not use From-Path for routing.
sections.plainLanguage: Before you can chat, the server wants to know who you are. You can show a pass from the website, answer a password challenge, or use a special certificate.

sections.title: Keeping the Connection Open
sections.content:
Clients and servers are RECOMMENDED to keep the WebSocket connection open by sending periodic WebSocket Ping frames. A browser page cannot control whether pings are sent, so that is up to each browser maker and its configuration.

When pings are not usable, an implementation MAY send bodiless MSRP SEND requests instead. Every client and server MUST be prepared to receive them.
sections.plainLanguage: If nobody talks for a while, the call might hang up. So each side sends a tiny 'still here?' nudge every so often.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
MSRP over WebSocket MUST be protected by a secure WebSocket connection (TLS over TCP). The client MUST authenticate the server's certificate using the WebSocket validation procedure of RFC 6455. Certificate name matching and cipher suite selection are handled by the browser, whose procedures supersede those in RFC 4975. TLS should follow the best current practices in RFC 7525.

The TLS session ends at the MSRP WebSocket Server, which can see the plain text. So the client (browser) SHOULD NOT indicate end-to-end security to the user.

Secure WebSocket protects the hop to the relay, not the whole path between the two chatting users.
sections.plainLanguage: The locked tunnel only goes as far as the helper in the middle. The helper can read the messages, so the app should not promise a secret between the two people.

data.title: Client handshake request
data.code:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: a.example.com
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==
Origin: http://www.example.com
Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: msrp
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13
